title: Rashi on Ketubot
text: Mishna: A virgin marries on the fourth day - It is a Rabbinical decree that she shall marry on the fourth day of the week as the Mishna will explain.
For twice in a week- it is discussing the maiden.

On the Second and the Fifth - It is one of the ten decrees established by Ezra, all of which are explained [on the Tractate] Bava Kamma chapter 'Meruba', and therefore [the sages]  decreed she shall marry on the fourth, for if there is any claim on her virginity he would wake up early to got to the Beit Din while his anger is still upon him. For if [more] time where to transpire in between, we could suspect that perhaps he might come to terms [with it] and cool down his mind, and will stand by her, and perhaps she cohabited [with someone else] while already under his domain (engaged to him), and she becomes forbidden to him, as we learn (Sota page 28a): and she secluded herself in secret and she became impure [to him], and by coming before the Beit Din [maybe] it will become clarified when the matter becomes public [lit. when the voice goes out], perhaps witnesses will come [to verify this possibility]. The Gemara objects and [argues they should be able to] marry on the first day of the week.
Gemara: seeing as it was taught, etc. - Later on an objection [is presented by the gemara] upon this.

The time came and she was not married - Later on in chapter 'Af al pi' (57a), it is taught from a mishna: A virgin is given twelve months from when the husband declares his desire for her, and gives notice concerning the marriage so as to let herself prepare the adornments/jewlery.  - L'farnes: in the foreign language [of Old French]: conréer [(to prepare, to equip, to adorn)].  - And to a widow, [she is given] thirty days.
Came the time - It[, the one established], and they did not marry in the Chupa. Later on [the gemara] will explain that it was the husband who held [the wedding] back.
They [f.] eat from [what is] his - That the husband is obligated to provide for his wide as decreed by the Beit Din, As [seen] later in chapter Na'ara, (Ketubot page 46b)

And they (f.) eat Terumah - If he is a Cohen and she is a daughter of Israel, since the cohen gives to his wife Terumah, as we learn (later in page 57b) from, "and a cohen, when he acquires a person..."
Mugmar – spices placed on fire, used to perfume the utensils and the garments.

He forbade us the betrothed women - this is by Rabbinic Law, for they decreed against seclusion with an unmarried woman, and even with one’s betrothed they did not permit it until she enters the wedding canopy, and with a blessing. As I have explained, a bride without a blessing is forbidden to her husband like a menstruant woman. And the Sages also instituted that we bless and say, ‘and He commanded us and forbade us,’ as we find with the Hanukkah lamp (Shabbat 23a)

The blessing over commandments - [for example,] for slaughtering and for circumcision. Since the entire thing is one expression of thanksgiving, and there is no interruption of any request in between, it does not require a closing formula, as it says in Arvei Pesachim (Pesachim 105a), the reason for blessings over commandments - what is it? Because it is an expression of thanksgiving, so too here, this entire blessing is likewise an expression of thanksgiving.

Since it is like Kiddush - because it is expressed in the language of sanctification - we conclude it with a closing formula, just as we do for Kiddush of the day, where we make a conclusion because there is an interruption in between, such as the phrase “for it is the first of the holy convocations.
New faces — on each day, people who were not there yesterday

When they soak barley in a basin – There are some who soak barley in a tub of water to produce beer for the needs of the wedding celebration. And there are others who say that for the sake of the bride and groom, they plant barley in a small pot, as a symbolic act, to say: “Be fruitful, multiply, and grow just like these barley plants."

He says: ‘I found an unobstructed orifice’ – and he does not have the claim of (absence of) blood. For example, she is from the family of Dorketi, who do not have virginal blood, as explained later (Ketubot 10b), or the bedsheet was lost from him and he does not know whether there was blood or not. But this point is clear to him: that he found the unobstructed orifice.

He is believed to forbid her to himself - and even though this matter cannot be clarified except through his own words, with respect to himself, he is believed, so as to render her forbidden to him like a piece of prohibited food. But to make her lose her ketubah, he is not believed.

“Younger than three years old—and now she is older, so her being seduced is considered consent and not coercion. Therefore, there is only one doubt: whether the act was rape or consensual. But there is not a second doubt - whether it occurred while she was still a virgin or not - because if she had been sexually penetrated earlier (before age three), her hymen would have grown back, as we learn in tractate Niddah (44b): ‘Younger than this is like putting a finger in the eye—the tear comes out and then returns.’”
He would write a bill of divorce for his wife- For if he died in war the bill would take effect retroactively from the day it was written-And it happened that Uriah [the Hittite] died in war.
For it is written-During the war of Shaul and your brothers etc. and David learned from his father Jesse to even lead [properly] like this when going out to war
Let him give it to her — why should we cause her to lose it, since he is giving it willingly?

Not in a case where he is making a claim about blood.. Rather, I can always say to you: when it’s a matter that he cannot verify, he is not believed to cause her to lose her ketubah. And the inference from the Mishnah, where we inferred, ‘but in the Galil he can make a claim’, that is referring to where he is making a claim about blood, and it is a case where they had  attendants who served them, so that there was no deception/overreaching in the matter: he did not see (blood), and it was lost. And that is a clear claim.

Rather, from inferior land - If she comes to collect her ketubah,  and he has superior land and inferior land, but no intermediate quality land, she cannot say, ‘Give me superior land or intermediate land at its equivalent value.’ Rather, if he comes to give her inferior land at its equivalent value, he may give it.

Reroute - When the bride comes out from her father's home to the wedding hall and (at the same time) those accompanying a dead body (for burial) and both groups will be shouting (one group with joy and the other in mourning) and we don't want to mix the two we reroute (those accompanying) the deceased (even) if it is to a different route.

For it is forbidden from a positive commandment - "So shall you bless" (Numbers 6). You [priests] and not non-priests. And a negative commandment that comes from a positive commandment is [called] a positive commandment.
Rabbi Shimon- In (3 chapters of the Talmud) More than, Covering the blood, It and it's offspring:

That is well with regards to idol worship - The offerings up of dead (euphemism for idol worship) and similarly the ox that requires to be stoned, that once judgment as been finalised it is forbidden to have any benefit from it, as we state in Bava Kama (45a) and Pesachim (22b) inferred from the verse 'it shall surely be stoned' do I not know that it will be come an (un-slaughtered) carcass, and a carcass etc.:
Mishne' I seduced - In the Gemara it will be explained why the author of the Mishne did not mention the case of I forced your daughter:

And he does not pay the penalty - In tractate Bava Kama we extrapolate that someone who admits his liability with regard to a fine is exempt from (paying it), (this is deduced) from (the verse) 'that which the judges make wicked' to exclude someone who makes himself wicked:
My ox killed someone - and I am liable to pay a redemption (fee):
Behold this one pays on his own volition - he (the author) holds a redemption fee is monetary compensation (as opposed to being a penalty):
The servant belon to someone - and I am liable to (pay) 30 sela:
He does not pay - as they (the 30 sela) are a penalty, [the proof of this is] that even if (the slave) was only worth one dinar he pays (lit. gives) 30 (sela)

Gem' That he did not tarnish her - the scandal of a victim of rape is not as significant as the scandal of seduction, and since it does not tarnish her (as much) we believe him (enough) to take from him compensation for embarrassment and depreciation on his admission (lit. mouth):
I may have said no - we do not believe him as this would reinforce the scandal:
We do not believe him - as this will publicise (lit. go out from him) a scandal that she is from the adulteresses in town:
She would prefer - to allow (lit. raise) the scandal, in order to gain financially [as she would now receive compensation]:
The family would not prefer - and it is not upon (within the ambit of) the court to do something that would reinforce their (the family's) embarrassment:
[Monetary - and would pay on his own (volition)]:

They do not stand in the presumptive status of safety (lit. being guarded) - if the owner does not (make effort) that they do not cause damage, [they are not in a presumptive status of naturally (lit. on their own) being safe (guarded) not to cause damage] rather they cause damage, even unusual methods of damage, therefore it is incumbent on their owner to guard them, and one who does not guard them, (should) legally pay all (the damage) but the Merciful One had mercy on him, however that which he pays he is paying legally:
In order that it should be guarded - that he should increase (his efforts) to guard it over (and above) his (basic) requirements to guard it:
We learn - in Bava Kama:

The victim and the damager (share) in the payment - both of them lose in the matter, the initial logic is that this is what it is saying, both of them are touched (lit. reached) with this loss, the victim loses half and the damager half:
That is how the damager is connected with the payment - that he loses half (by paying) with his money:
He is not taking his (entitlement) - That whatever he takes, is taken for free [he was not entitled to it in the first place]:
Is he contributing (lit. connected) with the payment? - (to be read) interrogatively (as a question):

GM' Wants 'to write' is not (the terminology) mentioned (in our Mishna) - Had the terminology (lit. learned) 'to write' (been used in the Mishna), we would not have deduced that the Toisefet (additional monies) are called Ketuboh (marriage contract) rather a gift given willingly, it would not have the legal status (lit. name or label) of a Ketuboh , now that (the Mishna) uses (lit. learns) the expression Lehoisif  (to add) it implies that it is additional to the Ketuboh, that the Rabbi's (lit. wise men) instituted, and has the legal status (lit name or label) of Ketuboh. Also he (Reb Aivu) supports it (this understanding) etc.:

Conditions of a Ketuboh (marriage contract) - Additional (funds) that are additional gifted to her, and similarly food and all those (various other conditional requirements of a Ketuboh) that were learnt in the chapter above:

One who sells and waives (her marriage contract) - sells her marriage contract or waives her marriage contract, waives and sells all of it (including the additional sum) and we don't say that the marriage contract is only the (basic) 100 (for a widow) 0r 200 (for a virgin):

For a rebellious (woman) - That we (will) learn in our chapter (further on 63a), that a woman that rebels against her husband [refusing to cohabit] etc., until when do we deduct [at the rate of 7 zuz per week], until the equivalent value of her marriage contract, (therefore) do not say the equivalent of the 100\200 alone rather we include the additional sum (to calculate the value of her marriage contract) how much we can deduct until it is all gone:
He has [assets] and doesn't want to support himself - from his own [assets] but rather only from Tzedaka and he afflicts himself with hunger
And how [big must they be]? One [breast] must be larger than her companion [the other breast], and it will be considered a blemish.

If so you are not Bar Levi- You are not worthy to have been announced [as such a righteous man]. As I hear, (that) a rainbow is solely a symbol of the covenant that the Earth will not be destroyed, and if there is a completely righteous person in a generation there is no need for a sign.
